label: Models Are the Lesson
notes: Open by stating the chapter's central thesis. Hyperbolic geometry is best learned by moving among models and watching which quantities survive the move. The deck follows printed pages 43 through 108: negatively curved surfaces, inversive and half-plane models, the hyperboloid and Klein models, hyperbolic computations, isometries, complex coordinates, and the geometry of the three-sphere.

label: Pseudosphere
notes: Begin with the pseudosphere. It has constant negative curvature but develops an edge and cannot be the whole hyperbolic plane. The lesson is that no surface embedded in Euclidean three-space realizes the entire hyperbolic plane isometrically. This failure motivates the move to intrinsic and projective models in the sections that follow.

label: Poincare Disk
notes: Move to the Poincare disk. Hyperbolic lines are Euclidean circles orthogonal to the boundary, and the model is conformal: angles are honest. The metric scale factor blows up near the boundary, which is why the same Euclidean segment is hyperbolically much longer near the edge. This is the conformal half of the inversive picture.

label: Half-Plane Model
notes: Present the upper half-plane model as the half-plane companion to the disk. Both are conformal. The metric scale is one over y, which makes the boundary the line at infinity. Mobius maps that preserve the upper half-plane are the isometry group, and parabolic, elliptic, and hyperbolic isometries are visible by their fixed-point behavior on the boundary.

label: Hyperboloid and Klein
notes: Add the hyperboloid model. Points sit on the upper sheet of a Minkowski hyperboloid, and the hyperbolic distance is recovered from the Minkowski inner product by an inverse hyperbolic cosine. Project from the origin to get the Klein disk model, where geodesics are straight chords but angles are distorted. Project to a paraboloid to recover the Poincare disk; both pictures are projections of the same hyperboloid.

label: Hyperbolic Computations
notes: Show that model changes are safe only when invariant formulas agree. In the hyperboloid model the points satisfy the Minkowski quadric, and cosh of the distance equals the negative inner product. The hyperbolic law of cosines is checkable numerically, and the chapter's invariant-check workflow is to verify the same number across two model representations.

label: Isometries and Complex Models
notes: Cover isometries. In the disk the isometry group is the group of Mobius transformations preserving the disk; in upper half-space it acts as PSL of two over the complex numbers. The Hermitian-form picture of hyperbolic three-space makes this action natural and connects to complex coordinates. This is the friend of hyperbolic geometry called complex projective.

label: Three-Sphere and Hopf
notes: Introduce the three-sphere as the positively curved friend. It is a homogeneous space with its own isometry group, and the Hopf fibration decomposes it into linked great circles. Stereographic projection lets us inspect several Hopf fibers in ordinary three-space. The chapter uses this to argue that three-dimensional geometry includes positive curvature alongside hyperbolic.

label: Disk Distance Lab
notes: Walk through the applied lab. Vary two points on the same Euclidean radius of the disk. Euclidean distance changes monotonically; hyperbolic distance reacts nonlinearly because of the metric scale factor. The table and plot make concrete the warning that Euclidean intuition inside the disk is useful only after the metric is included.

label: Recap
notes: Close with the chapter takeaways. The Poincare disk is conformal; the Klein disk straightens geodesics; the hyperboloid model makes distance algebraic. Negative curvature in Euclidean space is a local guide but not a global model. The three-sphere and Hopf flow show that three-dimensional geometry includes positively curved homogeneous models as well.
